headline: California: Interior ties Chico 'hemp' raid to public-land grows
dek: Interior says a BLM-led probe traced marijuana from grows on federal land to Chico's warehouses, and that two licensed hemp farms grew marijuana.
key_points: The Interior Department said on 25 November that the Bureau of Land Management led the investigation behind the 17 November Chico raid that seized about 235,661 pounds of marijuana.
BLM agents traced shipments to the warehouses from several grows, which investigators allege include sites on BLM and US Forest Service land.
In September and October, two large cultivation sites in Tehama and Butte counties holding California industrial hemp licences tested as marijuana; more than 7,500 pounds were seized.
On our arithmetic the haul is about 107 metric tonnes, and its stated street value equals roughly 29% of California's legal third-quarter retail sales.
body: The record marijuana seizure in Chico, California, was a federal case from the start, the US Department of the Interior said on 25 November. In a release, Interior said the investigation was led by the Bureau of Land Management's Office of Law Enforcement and Security, and that agents traced marijuana shipments into the Chico warehouses from several cultivation sites, including land managed by the BLM and the US Forest Service.

As we reported on 21 November, the Butte County Sheriff's Office announced that detectives, BLM agents and state investigators served a warrant on 17 November at industrial warehouses on Contractors Lane, where marijuana was being processed under the guise of hemp. They arrested 62 people and seized about 235,661 pounds, which the sheriff valued at $282.8 million. Interior's account adds the federal trail and two earlier hemp-licence seizures.

Interior describes the warehouses as the processing hub of a wider network that allegedly grew, processed and distributed marijuana across Northern California. Inside, investigators found equipment to process, de-stem and sort flower, with product packed in large crates and boxes. It took three days to document the evidence and remove the marijuana. Interior puts the haul at more than 117 tons and some outlets have used nearly 118 tons; both describe the same 235,661 pounds counted by the sheriff.

The release links the case to hemp licensing. In September and October 2026, investigators found two large cultivation sites in Tehama and Butte counties that held California industrial hemp licences. Testing confirmed the crops were marijuana, and more than 7,500 pounds were seized. The Drug Enforcement Administration's Sacramento office provided logistical support for the Chico warrant, along with the Butte Interagency Narcotics Task Force and the California Department of Cannabis Control.
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said the department 'will not tolerate criminals exploiting federal property'. The BLM remains the lead agency, and the investigation is continuing.

All 62 people found at the warehouses were booked into the Butte County Jail and charged with cultivating marijuana, according to the sheriff; two faced additional charges. CBS Sacramento reported that those arrested were aged 19 to 83, and that 34 gave Yuba City addresses, 14 Sacramento and six Chico. Several face possession-for-sale charges. So far, the charges announced are state charges booked by the Butte County Sheriff's Office, even though the BLM leads the wider investigation.
> The Chico case shows the hemp licence itself being used as cover, which is the problem regulators and lawmakers keep pointing to.

On our arithmetic, 235,661 pounds is about 107 metric tonnes, and the sheriff's $282.8 million estimate implies about $1,200 a pound. Street-value figures are law-enforcement estimates and run well above wholesale prices. Even so, they show the scale: California's licensed retailers sold about $987 million of cannabis in the third quarter of 2026, as we reported on 20 November, so the estimated value of one seizure equals roughly 29% of a quarter's legal sales.

For licensed operators, that is the point. Illicit supply on this scale undercuts legal prices across the state, and California's legal market carries a 15% excise tax plus sales tax that illicit sellers never pay.

The case lands as the federal definition of hemp is due to change on 11 December 2026, which would cap finished hemp products at 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container. Supporters of that change, including the 14 Republican senators who wrote to President Trump this week, argue the hemp loophole has been exploited by cartels and foreign operators, while the hemp industry and a bipartisan Senate bill favour a regulatory framework instead. Chico gives supporters of the change a concrete example: licensed hemp farms that were growing marijuana, and a hemp processing front that handled more than 100 tonnes.
It also raises a question for California's own hemp programme: how two large licensed hemp sites came to be growing marijuana, and what checks the licences carried.

Watch for federal charges, since the BLM leads the case and the alleged cultivation sites include federal land. Watch for any action by California regulators against the Tehama and Butte hemp licences. And watch 11 December, when the federal hemp change and the government funding deadline arrive together.
